content: To identify additional reviews not captured in the initial database search, a snowball searching method was employed. This involved screening the reference lists of included articles and consulting experts in the field. Two independent reviewers (BC and ML) screened the titles and abstracts of each reference based on predefined inclusion and exclusion criteria. Any discrepancies between the reviewers were resolved through a consensus meeting. If no agreement could be reached, a third reviewer (PC) was consulted. This process was conducted using the blinded online application Rayyan. The full-text screening for inclusion and exclusion criteria was also performed by two reviewers (BC and ML). Discrepancies during this stage were similarly resolved with the assistance of the third reviewer (PC). The methodological quality of the included systematic reviews was assessed using the AMSTAR 2 tool (A Measurement Tool to Assess Systematic Reviews). This 16-point tool evaluates the methodological rigor of systematic reviews. AMSTAR 2 has demonstrated strong inter-rater agreement, test-retest reliability, and content validity. Each item was rated as High, Moderate, Low, or Critically Low, with cut-off values of 100%, ≥75%, ≥50%, and below 50%, respectively. Two reviewers used AMSTAR 2 to assess the risk of bias in the included reviews. Reviews rated as Critically Low were excluded from further analyses, as they were deemed incapable of providing an accurate summary of the available evidence. Criterion-specific AMSTAR 2 credibility ratings, overall rating scores, and overall ratings for each included review were documented. Supplementary material 7 contains all relevant considerations. Abbreviations used include COI (conflict of interest), PICO (population, intervention, comparator, outcome), PY (partial yes), and RoB (risk of bias). The AMSTAR 2 tool evaluates several key aspects of systematic reviews, including: 1. Whether the research questions and inclusion criteria incorporated PICO components. 2. Whether the review methods were established prior to conducting the review and whether deviations from the protocol were justified. 3. Whether the authors explained their selection of study designs for inclusion. 4. Whether a comprehensive literature search strategy was employed. 5. Whether study selection was performed in duplicate. 6. Whether data extraction was performed in duplicate. 7. Whether a list of excluded studies was provided with justifications for exclusions. 8. Whether the included studies were described in adequate detail. 9. Whether a satisfactory technique was used to assess the risk of bias in individual studies. 10. Whether the sources of funding for included studies were reported. 11. If meta-analysis was performed, whether appropriate statistical methods were used for combining results. 12. If meta-analysis was performed, whether the potential impact of risk of bias in individual studies on the results was assessed. 13. Whether the authors accounted for risk of bias when interpreting or discussing the results. 14. Whether the authors provided a satisfactory explanation for and discussion of any observed heterogeneity. 15. If quantitative synthesis was performed, whether publication bias was adequately investigated and its impact discussed. 16. Whether the authors reported any potential sources of conflict of interest, including funding received for conducting the review. The total AMSTAR 2 score was calculated by dividing the total points by the number of questions answered. For example, the AMSTAR 2 tool was used in Shea et al. (2017) to critically appraise systematic reviews that included randomized or non-randomized studies of healthcare interventions. In the context of physical activity and health outcomes, systematic reviews and meta-analyses were conducted to evaluate the association between occupational physical activity (OPA) and various health outcomes, including all-cause mortality, cardiovascular disease, colon cancer, rectal cancer, and breast cancer. For all-cause mortality, the population studied included adults aged 18–64 years. The exposure was defined as the duration, frequency, and/or intensity of OPA or a compositional score reflecting total OPA volume. Comparisons were made with no OPA or lower levels of OPA. The outcome was all-cause mortality. Certainty assessments and findings were summarized, with considerations for study design, risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision, and other factors. For cardiovascular disease, similar parameters were assessed, with the outcome being cardiovascular disease incidence. Meta-analyses of observational data were conducted to evaluate the relationship between physical activity and stroke risk. For colon cancer, systematic reviews and meta-analyses examined the association between physical activity and colon cancer prevention. The reviews compared the highest versus lowest levels of physical activity and assessed heterogeneity, confounding factors, and methodological limitations. For rectal cancer, the reviews similarly evaluated the relationship between physical activity and cancer risk, with a focus on domain-specific physical activity and sedentary behavior. For breast cancer, meta-analyses of prospective studies assessed the association between physical activity and breast cancer risk. The reviews compared the highest versus lowest levels of physical activity and considered factors such as hormone replacement therapy. Across these reviews, methodological challenges included heterogeneity in study populations, variations in physical activity measurement, and confounding factors such as dietary intake. These limitations were acknowledged in the interpretation of findings.
